title: UGC drafting rules for foreign univ campuses here
excerpt: The University Grants Commission is drafting a policy to allow selected foreign universities to set up campuses in Bangladesh, as local private universities call for a level playing field.
body_html:
The University Grants Commission is drafting a policy to allow selected foreign universities to set up campuses in Bangladesh, as local private universities call for a level playing field.

Several universities from Australia, England and elsewhere have expressed interest, UGC Chairman Prof Mamun Ahmed told The Daily Star. The commission hopes to finalise the policy this year.

“But we will be very selective,” he said.

The UGC is considering restricting eligibility to universities ranked among the world’s top 100, 200 or 500, but no decision has been made.

The Association of Private Universities of Bangladesh (APUB) supports the entry of reputed foreign universities but wants them to meet requirements similar to those imposed on local institutions.

APUB Secretary General Ishtiaque Abedin said newer private universities could be the hardest hit, as many are still developing their campuses and struggling to attract students.

“If it is healthy competition, that is good for us,” he said, adding that foreign universities should establish proper campuses rather than operate poorly equipped study centres.

WHAT UGC IS CONSIDERING

The proposed policy will cover the operations of foreign universities, tuition fees and their arrangements with parent institutions.

Prof Mamun said local involvement would be mandatory, although its form has yet to be decided. Partnerships with Bangladeshi universities are among the options.

The UGC wants tuition fees to remain affordable but has yet to fix a ceiling or determine scholarship requirements.

It is also considering requiring parent universities to send faculty members to their Bangladesh campuses alongside locally recruited teachers. The ratio has yet to be decided.

Other proposals include allowing students to transfer midway through their programmes to parent campuses abroad, offering joint and dual degrees, and facilitating student and teacher exchanges.

Abedin said credit transfer arrangements must be clearly defined before admission, warning that students who complete two years in Bangladesh could face financial losses if parent universities recognise only one year’s credits.

He also said foreign institutions should operate on a non-profit basis, as local private universities must under the Private University Act 2010, and reinvest any surplus in Bangladesh.

He also suggested scholarships for disadvantaged students and partnerships between foreign and Bangladeshi universities.

APUB Secretariat Director Belal Ahmed said the association had not yet been consulted and called for private universities to be included in discussions before the policy is finalised.

EXISTING RULES DIFFER

Existing laws set different requirements for local private universities and foreign university branches and study centres.

Under the Private University Act 2010, local universities seeking initial approval must have at least 25,000 square feet of floor space, three faculties and six departments.

They must also maintain reserve funds of Tk 5 crore in Dhaka and Chattogram metropolitan areas, Tk 3 crore in other metropolitan areas and Tk 1.5 crore elsewhere.

To obtain a permanent charter, they must establish campuses on at least one acre of land in Dhaka and Chattogram metropolitan areas, or two acres elsewhere.

The law also requires universities to reserve 6 percent of admission places with fee waivers -- half for children of freedom fighters and half for poor and meritorious students from remote and underdeveloped areas.

Universities must also use their general funds to cover institutional expenses.

The 2014 regulations governing foreign universities, meanwhile, require branch campuses to have 25,000 square feet of floor space and study centres 10,000 square feet, in either owned or rented premises.

The required reserve funds are Tk 5 crore for branch campuses and Tk 1 crore for study centres.

Unlike the rules for local universities, the regulations have no permanent land requirement or international ranking threshold.

They also allow surplus funds to be shared among foreign universities, local representatives and entrepreneurs.

APUB wants the new policy to address these disparities so that foreign institutions do not receive preferential treatment.

PAST ATTEMPTS, NEW PUSH

In 2007, the UGC identified 56 unauthorised institutions operating as purported foreign university branches or affiliated centres amid allegations of degree-selling. Four challenged the decision in court.

The government introduced regulations for foreign universities in 2014 but suspended the approval process in November 2016.

The UGC later considered amendments, including a proposed ban on study centres.

A study centre linked to Monash College, approved in 2021, drew objections from APUB. Malaysia’s UCSI University, meanwhile, opened a branch campus in Dhaka in 2023.

In March this year, the UGC cited the 2014 regulations when ordering unauthorised branches and study centres to suspend operations and apply for approval by April 25.

Mamun said bringing reputed foreign universities to Bangladesh could help reduce spending on overseas education and attract students from neighbouring countries.

He advocated “brain circulation” rather than “brain drain”, with Bangladeshis studying abroad maintaining ties with the country.

The proposed policy would also cover Bangladeshi universities seeking to open campuses overseas.

The UGC also plans to launch a “Study in Bangladesh” portal, set up international offices, coordinate with relevant ministries and create a database of foreign students.

Prof Mamun said foreign campuses would be monitored to ensure their academic standards remained comparable to those of their parent universities.

“I hope we can finish it this year,” he said.
